analysis.one_liner: Funds removal of lead paint hazards in older homes and forces sellers and landlords to disclose them.
analysis.headline: Introduced with bipartisan support and a subcommittee hearing, the bill died in the Senate Banking Committee without ever reaching a floor vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would send federal grants to states and cities to find and remove lead paint hazards in pre-1978 housing, prioritizing low-income families with young children. It would require anyone selling or renting a pre-1978 home to hand buyers and tenants a lead hazard pamphlet, disclose any known lead hazards, and give buyers time to get the home tested. It would also require the government to inspect and clean up lead hazards in federally owned housing before selling it, and create a system of certified contractors and laboratories to do the work.
analysis.who_benefits: Families living in older homes with deteriorating lead paint — especially low-income and minority households, where the bill's own findings say lead poisoning is concentrated. The bill's findings state that as many as 3 million American children under age 6 are affected and that children in up to 3.8 million homes are endangered by chipping lead paint or lead dust. Renters and homebuyers would learn about hazards before signing a lease or contract, and communities would get grant money to abate the worst units.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Families with children in older homes

how_it_helps.text: Authorizes $250 million per year in grants to state and local governments to assess, control, and abate lead paint hazards in pre-1978 private housing, with selection criteria prioritizing risk to children under 6 and low-income families.

Requires sellers of pre-1978 homes to give buyers a lead hazard pamphlet, disclose any known lead hazards, and allow at least 10 days for a lead assessment before the buyer is bound to the contract; imposes fines and triple damages on knowing violators.
Requires inspection and abatement of lead hazards in all federally owned pre-1978 residential properties before the government disposes of them.
Creates a certified-contractor and certified-laboratory system for federally funded lead work, a national clearinghouse on lead poisoning, a public awareness campaign, and a lead hazard hotline.

Requires lead hazard assessment and reduction to be built into federal housing programs — FHA-insured loans, Section 8, HOME, and Community Development Block Grants — so abatement can be financed along with repairs.

analysis.who_pays: If enacted, the federal government would pay for the grants (up to $250 million a year, with a 10 percent local match). Owners and sellers of pre-1978 housing would bear the cost of disclosures, assessments, and any abatement needed to rent or sell, and those costs would partly flow into home prices and rents. Hand tool makers and home improvement retailers would carry small labeling and information duties.
analysis.who_pays_short: Taxpayers and owners of pre-1978 housing

drawbacks.text: The grants rely on new appropriations of $250 million for each of fiscal 1993 and 1994, a real federal cost at a time of budget pressure.

Disclosure and assessment duties add paperwork and legal exposure for sellers and landlords — knowing violators face fines up to $5,000 and triple damages — and the bill itself conditions mandatory rental assessments on a finding that they would not hurt the supply of affordable housing for families with children.
Abatement work done badly can raise lead dust exposure, which is why the bill requires periodic blood-lead and dust testing after grant-funded work and certification of contractors.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public health upside is large and well documented in the bill's own findings: millions of children exposed to lead, with lifelong learning and behavioral damage. The costs — federal grants with modest local matches, disclosure paperwork in real estate transactions, and abatement on units the government touches — are real but far smaller than the harms of inaction. The bill was drafted cautiously, phasing in disclosure rules over two to three years and building in a test for whether rental assessments would shrink affordable housing supply.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in March 1992, referred to the Senate Banking Committee, got one subcommittee hearing, and then sat there until the 102nd Congress ended in January 1993 — never reported out, never voted on.

narrative.text: Senator Alan Cranston introduced the bill on March 11, 1992, with original cosponsors including Republican Senator Alfonse D'Amato and Democrats Sarbanes, Kerry, Lieberman, and Akaka.
Nine senators cosponsored the bill — six Democrats and three Republicans.
On March 19, 1992, the Senate Banking Committee's Housing and Urban Affairs Subcommittee held hearings on the bill, printed as S.Hrg. 102-618.
No further action was taken; the bill remained with the Senate Banking Committee when the 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Owners and sellers of pre-1978 housing were spared new disclosure and abatement duties, while the families most exposed to lead paint got no relief.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Owners of older housing; families got nothing

sides.party_line_note: The sponsorship was bipartisan from the start — the bill's original cosponsors included a senior Republican, and the 9 cosponsors split 6 Democrats and 3 Republicans — yet the committee never acted on it.

industries.industry: Sellers and landlords of pre-1978 housing
industries.note: They would have to disclose known lead hazards, hand over assessment reports, give buyers 10 days to test, and face fines and triple damages for knowing violations. Their interest ran against buyers' and tenants' right to know what they were moving into.

industries.industry: Lead hazard assessment and abatement contractors and laboratories
industries.note: The bill would create a federal certification system and route grant-funded abatement work to certified firms. Their business would grow alongside the public health goal.

industries.industry: Mortgage lenders, private mortgage insurers, and federally chartered secondary mortgage institutions
industries.note: The bill would fold lead hazard costs into FHA underwriting and create a task force including lenders and mortgage insurers on private financing of abatement. Some new underwriting burden, but also a defined role in financing the work.

industries.industry: Home improvement retailers and hand tool manufacturers
industries.note: Retailers would distribute consumer information on renovation lead hazards, and makers of common remodeling tools would have to affix warning labels. Modest compliance costs in exchange for informed customers.
